subject: english-literature
title: Hardy's Wessex: Fate and the Fallen Woman
welcome_lead: Step into Thomas Hardy's 1891 novel and trace how rural tragedy, social hypocrisy, and cosmic indifference converge on a single 'Pure Woman'.
meta_desc: A-Level study adventure on Hardy's Tess of the D'Urbervilles: fate, fallen woman trope, paganism, and Victorian class.
final_note: Hardy's subtitle is a deliberate provocation: he asks Victorian readers to redefine purity itself.

concepts.def: A Victorian narrative figure marked by lost sexual 'purity' and consequent social ruin; Hardy interrogates and subverts it.
Hardy's controversial 1891 subtitle that defends Tess's moral purity against Victorian convention, sparking outrage on publication.

Hardy's semi-fictional reimagining of south-west England, a landscape that mirrors emotional and social states.

The Durbeyfields' decayed aristocratic lineage drives the plot, exposing late-Victorian anxieties about class and inheritance.

walkthroughs.body_html: Published serially in 1891 (Graphic) and as a volume the same year, Tess appeared as Victorian sexual mores were under increasing pressure. Hardy bowdlerised serial chapters to satisfy editors, restoring them for the volume. The subtitle 'A Pure Woman, Faithfully Presented' enraged critics like Mowbray Morris, who accused Hardy of 'succulent' immorality. The scandal contributed to Hardy abandoning prose for poetry after Jude the Obscure (1895).

walkthroughs.h2: Alec and Angel as Twin Destructions
walkthroughs.body_html: Alec d'Urberville embodies predatory, performative aristocracy; his religious conversion is theatrical and short-lived. Angel Clare, the freethinker, proves crueller: his rejection of Tess on their wedding night exposes the double standard he claims to reject. Critics from Penny Boumelha to Patricia Ingham read the two men as halves of a single patriarchal violence — body and mind — that destroys Tess.

Tess's arrest at Stonehenge ('a heathen temple, you say?') reframes her as a pagan sacrifice rather than a Christian sinner. Hardy's invocation of 'the President of the Immortals' (a phrase from Aeschylus) ends the novel with a deliberately Greek, fatalistic cadence, displacing Christian providence with classical tragedy.
